title: What belongs in a yacht management plan
excerpt: A useful management plan begins with the way you use your yacht, then gives every recurring task, decision, and update a clear place.

sections.heading: Begin with your calendar
sections.body: Before discussing a service schedule, describe the season you want to have. Note the months you expect to be aboard, the places you intend to visit, and the occasions that matter most. Include quieter periods, too. A yacht used every weekend needs a different rhythm from one awaiting a family holiday. These details give the management conversation a practical starting point and help establish priorities.

sections.heading: Make responsibility visible
sections.body: A clear plan describes what is included, how often it is arranged, and who is responsible for coordinating it. Interior care, exterior presentation, maintenance coordination, crew arrangements, and guest preparation may all involve different people. Ask how those people connect and where requests should go. One agreed point of contact, supported by a written scope, makes it easier to follow progress without managing every conversation yourself.

sections.heading: Agree on the update you need
sections.body: Decide what you would like to see in a regular update: completed work, upcoming visits, photographs, open decisions, or changes to the calendar. Agree which matters require your approval and how those requests will reach you. The right level of detail is personal. A concise, consistent report should let you understand the yacht's current position, ask informed questions, and prepare for your next time aboard.

title: A more considered departure checklist
excerpt: Thoughtful guest preparation starts well before arrival. A shared brief helps bring timing, preferences, provisioning, and the small details of your day together.

sections.heading: Set the shape of the day
sections.body: Begin with the essentials your management team and captain need for planning: your preferred date, arrival time, guest count, and the kind of day you have in mind. A relaxed lunch and a weekend away call for different preparation. Share your preferences early, while allowing the captain to determine operational arrangements. Keep one current itinerary so guests, crew, and anyone coordinating shore arrangements receive consistent information.

sections.heading: Record preferences once
sections.body: Build a simple guest brief with the details that make hosting easier. Think about meal preferences, dietary requirements, preferred refreshments, cabin arrangements, and any items you would like available on arrival. Confirm these details with guests instead of relying on last season's notes. Share personal information only with the people who need it for the trip, and keep the brief focused on useful, current requests.

sections.heading: Close the planning loop
sections.body: Before the visit, request a concise preparation update covering the arrangements you have agreed. Confirm arrival instructions, shore reservations, provisioning requests, and any decisions still awaiting your response. Keep owner and guest planning separate from the captain's operational checks. After your time aboard, note what worked and what you would change. Those observations help the next visit feel more familiar without turning every departure into a new planning exercise.

title: Planning a refit around your season
excerpt: A well-defined project starts with your next intended use. Work backward from that date to clarify scope, dependencies, decisions, and a realistic return window.

sections.heading: Define the result before the work
sections.body: Describe what you want to be different when the project is complete. Perhaps the interior should better suit longer stays, or several planned upgrades need to happen during the same yard period. Distinguish essential work from optional additions and discuss that distinction with your project coordinator. A written scope creates a shared reference for conversations with specialist providers and helps keep later decisions connected to your original priorities.

sections.heading: Give decisions room in the calendar
sections.body: Share your intended return date early, then ask for a schedule that identifies the decisions needed along the way. Materials, specialist availability, and the order of work can affect timing. Agree when selections and approvals are due, and discuss how changes will be handled. Leave space between the anticipated completion date and your first planned trip so the team can arrange the agreed handover and final preparations.

sections.heading: Plan the handover at the beginning
sections.body: Agree in advance how completion will be documented and who will review the finished work with you. Depending on the project, that may include progress photographs, provider records, updated manuals, or a list of remaining items. Ask your coordinator to distinguish completed work from anything still being resolved. A clear handover gives you an organized account of the project and a useful reference for future conversations about the yacht.
